text: What if a giant planet came drifting into our solar system, and passed right by Earth?
Not a comet. Not an asteroid. A whole planet, as big as Jupiter, with no sun of its own.
These rogue planets are real. Our galaxy may hold more of them than stars.
Year one. Astronomers spot it out past Neptune, racing toward us at twenty-six kilometres every second.
They check the numbers again and again. It won't hit us. It will miss Earth by ten million kilometres.
Sounds safe? That's only twenty-six times farther than the Moon. And this thing weighs as much as three hundred Earths.
Year five. It's the brightest thing in the night sky after the Moon. With binoculars, you can see its stripes.
The week of the pass, it grows bigger than the full Moon. Nobody sleeps. Everyone is outside, staring up.
But its gravity tugs on Earth even harder than the Moon does. Tides surge, and seaside towns are told to leave.
Scientists even watch for earthquakes, because strong tides can tip faults that are ready to slip.
Then, in just a few days, it's gone. But it takes something with it.
Its pull drags Earth's whole orbit, by up to three percent.
A little closer to the Sun, and Earth could get hotter than any climate forecast.
A little farther, and we could slide into an ice age. Even the year could change by two weeks.
And all of that, from a planet that never even touched us.
Right now, billions of rogue planets may be drifting through our galaxy. None is known to be heading our way.
But if one ever did, would you stay up all night to watch it pass?
